genre: political philosophy and social science essay
centralQuestion: What remains of the partnership-domination idea when we refuse to romanticize the past?
thesis: Domination and partnership are recurrent coordination equilibria; technology and institutions change their relative cost without abolishing either repertoire.

narrativeFramework.why: A nearly forty-year-old idea claims societies keep organizing around partnership or domination. Two Ways to Build a World keeps Riane Eisler's contrast and drops the peaceful golden age. It treats domination and partnership as two recurring ways people coordinate under power. Its central claim is that technology and institutions change which way is cheaper.
narrativeFramework.how: Instead of labelling whole civilizations, the book measures relationships along distinct dimensions. It asks who can leave, speak, appeal, observe decisions, and impose sanctions. Domination appears when wealth, media, office, and force convert into each other until escape disappears. Hierarchy can stay legitimate when its purpose, scope, duration, review, and exit are clear.
narrativeFramework.what: Drawing on commons governance, it shows cooperation needs boundaries, monitoring, graduated sanctions, and appeal. Artificial intelligence can become an empire machine, or it can lower the cost of partnership. Start with Chapter 3, From Binary to Coordinate System, and learn to map who holds power.

spans.quote: Two Ways to Build a World — Ten-minute edition Two Ways to Build a World Ten-minute edition The book revisits Riane Eisler’s partnership–domination distinction without relying on a peaceful prehistoric golden age. It treats the two patterns as ways to coordinate people: one can make refusal costly, while the other makes contribution, reciprocal rules, and contestable authority worthwhile. Neither is pure, and neither belongs to one period or ideology. The question is which material, social, institutional, and technical conditions make each pattern more likely. 1. The idea that refuses to die Eisler’s historical account remains contested, yet her analytical contrast can still be useful. The book separates an empirical question about migration and prehistoric violence from a more general question: why does one social order reward coercion while another rewards contribution? Read this chapter in the complete edition 2. The past is not a moral exhibit Archaeology neither establishes a uniformly peaceful Old Europe nor makes domination inevitable. Ancient DNA, graves, settlement patterns, and inequality measures support different inferences with different limits. The useful questions concern control of resources, violence, exit, office, and surplus. Read this chapter in the complete edition 3. From binary to coordinate system Partnership and domination describe dimensions of relationships, not whole civilizations. Examine who can leave, speak, appeal, observe decisions, impose sanctions, and convert one advantage into many forms of control. A hierarchy can be necessary and still remain bounded and contestable. Read this chapter in the complete edition 4. Two roads to status Influence can grow through dominance, backed by fear and the capacity to impose costs, or through prestige, granted because others value competence. Prestige can later be converted into coercive office. The crucial design problem is preventing one kind of status from governing unrelated domains. Read this chapter in the complete edition 5. Equality is something people do Egalitarian orders require active counter-power rather than an absence of ambitious people. Coalitions, criticism, courts, labor organization, replication, exit, and protected voice can restrain would-be monopolists. Formal consent says little when refusing destroys a person’s livelihood and membership at once. Read this chapter in the complete edition 6. Cooperation is not innocence Durable cooperation needs boundaries, memory, monitoring, and proportionate sanctions. Shared resources cannot be governed by goodwill alone, yet enforcement need not become unchecked central command. The institutional task is to make rule-breaking answerable without giving enforcers permanent arbitrary power. Read this chapter in the complete edition 7. The tribal trap Human solidarity can coexist with exclusion of outsiders. In-group cooperation is not automatically partnership across group boundaries. The book asks whether rules protecting members also constrain how they treat strangers, rivals, and vulnerable people beyond the group. Read this chapter in the complete edition 8. Surplus, storage, and chokepoints Stored resources and narrow gates can make power durable. Whoever controls grain, land, payment rails, cloud infrastructure, or discovery can command more than their visible holdings suggest. Technology may move chokepoints rather than abolish them. Read this chapter in the complete edition 9. Why threat loves hierarchy Emergencies can justify concentrated authority for a limited task. The danger comes when emergency powers outlive the threat, leaders benefit from keeping fear salient, and dissent loses protection. Reversal, expiry, and independent review matter before the crisis arrives. Read this chapter in the complete edition 10. Scale changes the game Personal trust weakens as strangers and specialized roles multiply. Large-scale cooperation needs procedures, records, rights, and institutions that replace knowledge of each individual. Scale does not force domination, but it raises the cost of keeping authority visible and contestable. Read this chapter in the complete edition 11. Every age has its power technology Horses, writing, guns, printing, networks, and models change who can coordinate, monitor, persuade, and resist. The same invention can strengthen concentrated command and distributed cooperation. Political outcomes depend on the surrounding rules, not the tool alone. Read this chapter in the complete edition 12. Partnership needs teeth The book draws on commons governance to show that cooperation requires clear boundaries, locally appropriate rules, monitoring, graduated sanctions, appeal, and nested institutions. Partnership is neither unlimited trust nor the absence of enforcement. Read this chapter in the complete edition 13. Hierarchy without domination The objective is not flatness. Task-specific authority can be legitimate when its purpose, scope, duration, review, and exit are clear. Hidden hierarchies can be harder to contest than declared ones. Expertise in one domain must not silently become power over every domain. Read this chapter in the complete edition 14. A diagnostic for real institutions A practical scorecard examines coercion, exit, voice, information, sanctions, status conversion, time, and boundaries. The point is to expose mixed patterns and surprising weaknesses rather than sort favored institutions into moral boxes. Read this chapter in the complete edition 15. How partnership fails Cooperative orders can drift toward oligarchy, procedural overload, charismatic capture, moral purity, or free-riding. Success creates assets worth capturing. Repair requires institutions that keep their own leaders, experts, and guardians open to challenge. Read this chapter in the complete edition 16. AI can become an empire machine AI can lower the cost of prediction, persuasion, surveillance, classification, and administrative action. Combined with concentrated data and infrastructure, these capabilities may turn many chokepoints into one computational layer. The book treats this as an institutional risk, not an unavoidable destiny. Read this chapter in the complete edition 17. AI can lower the cost of partnership The same tools can help people read rules, inspect contracts, translate, verify claims, deliberate, and coordinate locally. Their value for partnership depends on traceability, access, portability, and the ability to contest machine-assisted decisions. Read this chapter in the complete edition 18. Designing a non-utopian future A serious design starts with human ambition, tribalism, error, crisis, and exploitation. Make domination expensive, visible, narrow, and reversible; make cooperation easier to sustain at scale. The closing claim is architectural: institutions can change which form of coordination is cheaper. Read this chapter in the complete edition The two appendices The appendices offer an institutional scorecard and a research agenda rather than a single score for a society. Readers can use them to test the framework against evidence, especially where archaeology or new technology might otherwise invite a simple moral story. Read the appendices in the complete edition
